title: Gulf Airspace Closures and Flight Cancellations Disrupt Travel for Millions of Indians Across the Middle East
excerpt: Kuwait, Bahrain, and UAE face widespread aviation disruptions as military activity forces airspace restrictions, with EASA advising airlines to avoid Gulf routes until July 29.
body:
• Kuwait temporarily closed its airspace on July 18 after intercepting missiles and drones, forcing Kuwait Airways to reschedule most flights affecting routes to India, Bangladesh, and beyond.
  • The European Aviation Safety Agency has advised airlines to avoid airspace over the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, and Kuwait at all altitudes until July 29, disrupting one of the world’s busiest aviation corridors.
  • Emirates and Etihad continue operating most routes from UAE airports, but several foreign carriers have suspended Dubai and Abu Dhabi services through October 2026.
  • An estimated 3.5 million Indian nationals live in the UAE alone, with millions more across the Gulf states depending on air connectivity to India.

Kuwait Airspace Shutdown Triggers Regional Chaos

Kuwait’s armed forces temporarily closed the country’s airspace on Saturday, July 18, after intercepting hostile aerial targets during an ongoing military escalation involving the United States and Iran. The closure forced Kuwait Airways to reschedule the majority of its flights, creating immediate disruption for passengers on routes connecting Kuwait City with destinations across India, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, Turkey, Egypt, and the United Kingdom.

The shutdown came after Kuwait’s military warned residents that explosions could result from defensive interceptions. Operations at Kuwait International Airport were running on reduced capacity even before the latest closure, with Terminal 1 already shut and flights consolidated into Terminals 4 and 5 for Kuwait Airways and Jazeera Airways respectively.

Air India Express, which operates significant capacity between Kuwait and Indian cities, was among the carriers forced to adjust schedules. Passengers have been advised to verify departure times, operating terminals, and connection status directly with airlines before traveling to airports.

EASA Issues Sweeping Airspace Warning

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency issued an emergency Conflict Zone Information Bulletin directing all covered operators to completely avoid the flight information regions of the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, and Kuwait at every altitude. The advisory also covers the western section of the Gulf of Oman within Muscat’s flight-information region and remains in effect until July 29, 2026, unless reviewed earlier.

EASA identified missile and drone activity, defensive interceptions, falling fragments, and the risk of aircraft misidentification as major hazards. The recommendation does not automatically ground every airline worldwide, but European carriers and operators under EASA authorization may cancel services or reroute aircraft significantly, producing different schedules among airlines serving the same destinations.

“Passengers should verify the operating terminal, departure time and connection status directly with the airline before travelling to the airport.”

— Kuwait Airways advisory, July 18, 2026

UAE Airlines Keep Flying as Foreign Carriers Pull Back

In a notable divergence, UAE-based carriers have maintained most operations. Emirates, Etihad Airways, flydubai, and Air Arabia continue flying across the majority of their route networks from Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Sharjah, and Ras Al Khaimah, though selected Bahrain and southern Saudi Arabia services face temporary disruptions.

Several foreign airlines have taken a more cautious approach. Multiple international carriers have extended suspensions of Dubai and Abu Dhabi services into August, September, and even October 2026, based on independent safety assessments. This split creates a confusing situation for travelers, where the same destination may be served by local carriers but not by European or other international airlines.

Retaliatory strikes from Yemen have also forced the emergency shutdown of four major airports in southern Saudi Arabia — Abha, Jizan, Najran, and Sharurah — further compressing available air corridors. Reports of GPS spoofing across the upper Gulf have added another layer of concern for aviation safety officials.

Impact on Indian Diaspora

The Gulf region is home to the largest concentration of Indians abroad. An estimated 3.5 million Indian nationals live in the UAE, with significant populations in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, and Oman. Air connectivity between India and the Gulf is among the densest in the world, with airlines operating hundreds of daily flights between Indian cities and Gulf destinations.

The disruptions come during peak summer travel season, when many Gulf-based Indian workers travel home for vacations and family visits. The US State Department has issued elevated travel advisories and maintained ordered departure mandates for non-essential staff and families at regional diplomatic posts, while the US Embassy in Bahrain has temporarily suspended routine consular services.

What Travelers Should Do

Aviation analysts expect disruptions to continue as long as the regional military situation remains volatile. Travelers with upcoming Gulf flights should monitor airline communications closely, consider booking backup routing through airports outside the affected zone, and maintain contact with embassy and consular services. Travel insurance providers have begun treating parts of the Gulf as active conflict zones, which may affect coverage terms for new bookings.
